name: SwAV (Swapped Assignments)
analogy: Think of it as two scouts looking at differently disguised copies of one chart, each sorting it into one of 32 filing drawers. They then swap answers: scout one must predict the drawer scout two chose, and the other way round. Drawers have to be used evenly, so no single drawer can hold everything.

steps.title: Make several altered views of each window
steps.description: A window of bars is copied a few times and each copy is changed in ways that should not alter its meaning, such as noise, small rescaling, hidden bars or a shorter crop. The copies come from the same window.
steps.inExample: A 48-bar MNQ window gets view A with noise and view B with 15 percent of bars masked.

steps.title: Describe each view as a short vector
steps.description: A network reads each view and a small head shrinks it to a short vector scaled to unit length. This vector is the view's position on the model's internal map.
steps.inExample: Each view becomes a vector of 128 numbers.

steps.title: Hold a set of prototypes
steps.description: The model keeps a fixed number of learned prototype vectors, one per drawer. Comparing a view's vector with each prototype tells how close the view is to each drawer. These prototypes are learned along with the network.
steps.inExample: 32 prototypes are held, each a 128-number vector, and every view is scored against all 32.

steps.title: Assign each view to drawers, evenly
steps.description: Within a batch the scores are turned into a soft assignment of each view across the drawers, with a rule that spreads the batch roughly evenly across drawers. This even-use rule stops the trivial answer of putting every window in the same drawer.
steps.inExample: View A of today's window puts 71 percent on drawer 7 and the rest on neighbouring drawers.

steps.title: Swap and predict
steps.description: The assignment computed for view A is used as the answer key for view B, and the assignment from view B is used as the key for view A. Each view must predict the other's drawer, so both must capture what the window is, not how it was disguised.
steps.inExample: View B is trained to put its probability on drawer 7, the drawer view A chose, and vice versa.

steps.title: Use the drawers and the vectors afterwards
steps.description: After training, the drawers give data-driven market states, and the encoder's vector for a window can feed other models. Each drawer is a recurring kind of window that can be inspected on the chart.
steps.inExample: Drawer 7 turns out to contain quiet upward-drifting mornings with below-average volume.

useFor.example: Sorting years of MNQ 5-minute windows into 32 drawers and studying what each drawer looks like.
Using the drawer number as a regime feature for a downstream model, alongside the 151 indicators.
Learning window descriptions without needing a huge batch of wrong examples.

useFor.task: Spotting windows that fit no drawer
useFor.example: Flagging windows whose probability is spread thinly across drawers as unlike anything seen before.

avoidWhen: You already know the regimes you care about and have labels for them; a supervised classifier gives you those exact classes.
Real market states are very uneven in frequency; forcing windows to spread evenly across drawers can split a common state or merge rare ones.

example.scenario: A researcher trains SwAV on two years of unlabelled MNQ 5-minute windows with 32 drawers. They then take the current morning window and read which drawer it falls in and how confident the assignment is.

input.summary: One window of bars with altered views, scored against 32 learned prototypes.

fields.name: window length
fields.meaning: Four hours of trading described to the model.

fields.name: number of drawers
fields.meaning: How many recurring window types the model sorts into.

fields.name: vector length
fields.meaning: The size of the window description compared with each prototype.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The recent typical bar travel, low for this time of day.

output.summary: A drawer assignment with probabilities, and a description of the window.

fields.name: most likely drawer
fields.meaning: The recurring window type the model assigns to this window.

fields.name: probability on drawer 7
fields.meaning: How much of the assignment sits on that drawer.

fields.name: second most likely drawer
fields.meaning: The runner-up, showing how clearly the window belongs to one type.

fields.name: window description
fields.meaning: The vector available to other models.

example.reading: A 71 percent assignment means the window sits clearly in drawer 7. The drawer has no meaning until you look at its members and at what followed them. Use it as a regime feature only if returns differ between drawers on data not used to learn them, across walk-forward folds.
